titulo.texto: Warrior with Basketry Armor and Club

frase_gancho.texto: A clay warrior with a helmet and armor, guarding the door of a tomb.

puente_narrativo.texto: After the warrior, the couple. Look for two figures seated side by side, with painted faces and large rings in their noses and ears.

guion_corto.texto: This clay warrior, about forty centimeters tall, comes from Jalisco and was made about two thousand years ago. He stands firm, with his mouth open, as if shouting. He wears a conical helmet, armor that covers his torso, and a club he seems about to swing. Notice the details: the ear ornaments, the marked pupils, and the lines of the breastplate, which imitate a woven fabric. Figures like this were placed in shaft tombs, at the entrance of the chamber, as guardians. They are not a battle scene, but the protection of the deceased. The body is hollow, in reddish and cream tones.

guion_largo.texto:
Look at his mouth. It is open, not to speak or to sing, but to shout. This warrior has a fixed gaze and a body ready to strike, even though he has not moved in two thousand years.

The armor is the most interesting part. What it was made of is debated: some specialists describe it as a braided weave of reed or fibers; others, as quilted cotton. Both systems existed in Mesoamerica. The Mexica used the ichcahuipilli, a quilted cotton armor, so effective against arrows that the Spaniards themselves adopted it and called it escaupil. The metal armor they had brought was far more uncomfortable in the tropical heat.

Notice also the helmet, conical in shape and with straps under the chin, and the wide guard around his neck. Each piece protects a part of the body: the head, the throat, the chest. He is a warrior designed with care, dressed to survive combat.

And the club, with bulges at the top, is a real weapon: a wooden club for striking. The warriors of West Mexico also used slings, spears, and darts. That there are armed figures in the tombs tells us that military elites existed, perhaps because people competed for fertile lands and for valuable materials such as obsidian, the volcanic glass you saw in the blades of Teotihuacán.

But this figure does not recall a specific battle. It is thought to protect. It was placed at the entrance of the burial chamber, as a guardian of the door, alongside dogs and vessels. Whoever wanted to enter had to get past him. He is like a watchman who stays to look after a house that no one will ever open again.

Each region of West Mexico had its own style. Colima, with its rounded, polished figures, like the [dogs](mna_s10_perros_colima) you saw. Nayarit, with expressive figures full of color, like the couple that comes next. Jalisco, with more angular, sharply marked features, like this warrior. All three are part of the same shaft tomb tradition, but each with its own character. If you learn to recognize them, you will be able to tell which region a figure comes from without looking at the label.

It is interesting to compare this warrior with the ones you already know. The [Eagle Warrior](mna_s06_guerrero_aguila) in the Mexica Hall and the [Atlantean figures of Tula](mna_s05_atlante_tula) are ideals of power: warriors who represent gods or the armies of enormous cities. This one, by contrast, is a modest guardian, made of clay, for a family tomb. And even so, it has the same intensity.

West Mexico, by the way, had a sense of humor. In other display cases there are figures that drink, that dance, that embrace, that carry a child or play ball. The warrior is serious because his job required it. But the world he comes from was a cheerful one.

And one last look at the expression. The eyes with marked pupils, the open mouth, the round ear ornaments: the sculptor wanted the guardian to look alive, alert. It is one of the finest examples of how clay, in the hands of a skilled craftsman, can seem about to move.

texto: Look at the open mouth: is he shouting or singing?
Notice the weave of the armor and the helmet
Find the club: how does he hold it?

texto.pregunta: Myth: These warrior figures show real battles.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were symbolic guardians of the tomb. Their function was to protect the deceased.
